newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian bonds lifted by EMU hopes, to hold steady.
newsitem.headline: Belgian bonds lifted by EMU hopes, to hold steady.

text.p: Belgian government bonds (OLOs) and futures found back their old selves again on Tuesday, shaking off selling pressure from across the Atlantic and from locals looking for a correction, dealers said.

The market bounced higher with other European markets which advanced on a wave of renewed hope for the punctual start of a broad EMU inspired by EU comments that the Maastricht three percent deficit/GDP target need not be applied strictly.
Buying emerged as players saw tensions over which country would be in and which out on which terms, particularly between France and Germany, ebbing away.
"There was not much volume, although a lot was seen in the 10-year benchmark," a trader said, adding he counted on the market holding current levels in the run-up to next week's U.S. report US-ECI.
"Normally we should hold these levels, although this is about as high as we can go," he said.

The benchmark OLO BE286= yielded 5.76 percent at 1530 GMT, just one basis point above a level identified by players as a trigger for profit-taking. The yield was down five basis points on Monday's late levels.
The spread over 10-year Bunds widened by one bp to eight with OLOs as per the norm lagging Bunds on the way up, but it remained relatively tight.
The tight spread over Bunds, disadvantageous funding and the remote risk of an EMU delay meant there was not much upside in being long OLOs against Bunds now, JP Morgan said in a report.

It expected the spread to rise marginally to over 10 basis points in the coming weeks, noting in its Market Views that the yield differential was stuck in a tight range and that independent yield curve moves by OLOs were non-existent.

Dealers said Bunds advanced after the future broke above 101.43. The German September contract FDBc1 was up 0.41 at 101.70 at 1540 GMT, its Belgian equivalent BGBc2 up 0.12 at 120.86. The Belgian future benefitted somewhat from rollover business out of June which expires on Wednesday.

Dealers focused on expectations for unchanged U.S. rates in the short term and on the June jobs report. OLOs and futures needed signs of stronger growth and inflation for a correction, dealers said. Evidence of strength was more likely to come from the buoyant U.S. than from sluggish Europe, they noted.
